title: ORDER BY Without an Index Adds a Sort
description: An ORDER BY on an unindexed column adds an expensive Sort; an index that stores rows in that order removes it. Why it matters: sorting is one of the most common operations in any reporting query, and an unindexed sort is one of the most common reasons a report gets slower every month.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is about what happens when you ask the database to hand back rows "in order," but nothing in the table is actually stored in that order. Even if your query only wants a small number of rows, an `ORDER BY` on an unsorted column can force SQL Server to sort the *entire* table first.

Why does this happen? A table's rows live on disk in whatever order its clustered index defines (often by an ID column) — not in whatever order your `ORDER BY` asks for. If you ask for the 100 cheapest products sorted by `Price`, but nothing keeps the rows in price order, SQL Server has no shortcut: it must first pull every row, sort all of them by price, and only then peel off the top 100.

Think of a classroom of 200,000 students lined up by student ID number. If a teacher asks "line up the 20 shortest kids, shortest first," there's no way to do that instantly — someone has to measure everyone, then physically re-sort the whole line, and only then read off the first 20. That's the expensive **Sort** operator you'll see in the query plan. The fix is to build an index that's already sorted the way you need — then "shortest first" is just reading off the front of an already-sorted line, no re-sorting required.

## Scenario
`SELECT TOP (100) ProductId, Price FROM Products ORDER BY Price` returns the 100 cheapest products. The plan has an expensive **Sort** operator even though you only want 100 rows.

## Why it's slow
Nothing stores the rows in `Price` order, so to find the smallest 100 SQL Server must **sort all 200k rows** at run time (a *Top N Sort*). Sorting is CPU- and memory-heavy and, on bigger inputs, can spill to tempdb.

## What to look for
- A **Sort** (often *Top N Sort*) operator, typically the most expensive node in the plan.

## The concept
An index is a **pre-sorted** structure. With an index on `Price`, the rows are already in order, so the optimizer just reads the first 100 from the index and skips the Sort entirely. Indexes don't only speed up `WHERE` — they also satisfy `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, `TOP`, and `MIN`/`MAX` by providing order for free.
startingQuery: SELECT TOP (100) ProductId, Price FROM Products ORDER BY Price;
hints: The Sort operator is doing the work — where would pre-sorted rows come from?
There is no index on Price, so all 200k rows are sorted at run time.
Create an index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Products_Price ON Products(Price);
